catalog_quote: [Dyachkov 2014 §1.3, p. 5] В томо-кан существует два базовых тоновых регистра – высокий (здесь и далее будет обозначаться как H) и низкий (L). [Heath 2014 §3.2.2, p. 7] The metrically weak position is the second syllable in CvCvCv(…). We see this especially in combinations of CvCv verb stems with -Cv(…) suffixes, whether derivational or inflectional. Depending on the stem-medial C and the suffix-initial C, this CvCv-Cv remains as such, syncopates to CvC-Cv, or truncates to Cv-Cv or Cv:-Cv. [Heath 2014 §3.7.1.3, p. 19] Uncompounded noun stems, which may have from one to three syllables, can be lexically {L}, {H}, or {LH}. This tone contour is heard in isolation, as the first word in a clause (when not subject to a following tonosyntactic controller), and before the 'it is' clitic (which lengthens the final syllable). The lexical contour is overridden by a special possessor-controlled contour, {H} for monosyllabics and {LH} for longer stems, when the noun is preceded by a second or third person possessor (including all nonpronominal-NP possessors). [Dyachkov 2021, p. 254] В томо-кан различаются два уровня тонов – высокий (H) и низкий (L). Примечательной особенностью томо-кан на фоне остальных языков догон является сложная тоносинтаксическая система, в которой тоновые характеристики словоформы могут зависеть, во-первых, от ее синтаксического статуса, а во-вторых, от ритмических правил.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked under (all with text layers; no scanned). (1) line 235 (sec. 1.3 'Система тонов', p.5): 'В томо-кан существует два базовых тоновых регистра – высокий (здесь и далее будет обозначаться как H) и низкий (L).' — verbatim as quoted. Ch.1 Phonology otherwise = consonant/vowel charts and sec.1.4 tone-overlay headings only. a full-text search for stress/accent ударен|акцент|stress|accent over the 154-pp. text: one hit, 'акцентуирующего' (discourse emphasis of a plural suffix), nothing on word stress. The draft does refer to a 'второй (слабый) слог' (pp.63, 70, 83, 105) and once to 'второго слабого и третьего сильного' syllable (p.106) as the site of rhythmic stem truncation before l-i…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tomo Kan is described purely as a two-level tone language (H, L; noun stems lexically {L}, {H}, {LH}; verb stems with A/E vocalic grades; extensive tonosyntactic overlays plus Tomo-Kan-specific left-to-right 'rhythmic' tonal dissimilation). No source opened states anything about word stress or accent; the only prominence-like remark is that the second syllable of CvCvCv strings is 'metrically weak' (site of syncope/truncation), i.e. a trochaic stem shape, stated by Heath (2014 §3.2.2) and echoed by Dyachkov (2014 p. 63 'второй (слабый) слог').
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress rule given). Tonal: Dyachkov 2016 notes the rhythmic dissimilation principles are tendencies with counter-examples in the corpus.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone described at stem/word level with phrase-level (NP, clause) tonosyntactic overlays; citation/isolation forms give lexical melodies. Dyachkov's data: Ségué village dialect (southern cliffs), with occasional notes on Djanga-Sagou; Heath's draft from his own assistant (village not stated in the pages read).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Tomo Kan proper (tomo1243, ISO dtm). Dyachkov's drafts and articles are based on the Ségué village dialect (southern cliffs, Mali), with occasional notes on Djanga-Sagou; Heath's 2014 draft does not name the village in the pages read. Not to be confused with Togo Kan / Tengu Kan (Tene Kan, dtk), for which Heath 2015 is a separate published grammar.
